summary: Proposes a new Routing Policy Specification Language attribute so a network can advertise an IP address that is reachable and can be used for diagnostic tests like pings. This helps debug intermittent reachability for new connectivity. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5943 defines an RPSL attribute for publishing an IP address that other network operators can use for diagnostic tests. The RFC recommends limiting probes to reduce the risk of overloading that address.

subtitle: An RPSL attribute for publishing an address that peers can use for diagnostic tests.

tldr.problem: When new IP connectivity is deployed, intermittent reachability can be difficult to diagnose from outside the network.
tldr.mechanism: A network advertises a pingable address inside a route or route6 object so other operators can test reachability and Path MTU discovery.
tldr.outcome: The attribute identifies a target for external diagnostics, with a recommendation to limit tests to ten probes in a five-minute window unless arranged otherwise.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 5943's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC defines an RPSL attribute for advertising addresses for external diagnostic testing.

sections.title: A Known Address for Network Tests
sections.content:
New IP connectivity can have intermittent reachability for reasons outside this RFC's scope. A network can publish a reachable address as a target for diagnostic checks such as ping and Path MTU discovery.

The document adds the optional, multi-valued pingable attribute to RPSL route and route6 objects. It also defines an optional ping-hdl contact handle for questions about the address.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can publish an address that peers may test from outside. The same route record can include a contact for questions about that address.

sections.title: Using the Pingable Address
sections.content:
The address must fall within the IP range advertised by the route or route6 object containing the attribute. Its presence signals that the network operator offers it for external diagnostic testing.

Tests should be limited to no more than ten probes in a five-minute window unless prior arrangements have been made with the attribute's maintainer.
sections.plainLanguage: The published test address must belong to the route that lists it. The RFC asks testers to keep probe rates low unless they have arranged otherwise.

sections.title: Protecting the Advertised Address
sections.content:
Publishing an address signals that an ICMP Echo Request and Echo Response service is available there. Other services may also run at the same address, at the operator's discretion.

The RFC warns that users may ignore the recommended probe limit and encourages operators to add their own rate limiting. It also recommends filtering services, protocols, and ports that are not intended for external users.
sections.plainLanguage: A public test address can attract more traffic than intended. Operators can rate-limit probes and block other services that should not be exposed.
